title: Blessings
hook: homes, cars, throats, animals, fields: almost anything can be blessed

segments.voice: Yesterday, a small font of holy water by the front door, touched on the way out and on the way back in. Your line was going out blessed. Did your fingers find the water, or the habit? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-two.

A church parking lot on a weekend morning. A priest in a white stole walks down a row of cars with a bucket and a sprinkler, and the drivers stand by their open doors. A few weeks later, the same priest is on the church steps with a line of dogs, a cat in a carrier, a goldfish in a jar and one very patient rabbit. Another day, people come forward after Mass and he holds two crossed candles at each throat. A farmer asks him out to a field. A young couple asks him over to a new apartment that still smells of paint. Cars, pets, throats, fields, kitchens. Is there anything the Church won't bless? That's today.
screen: `A ROW OF CARS AND A SPRINKLER.` → `A LINE OF DOGS AND ONE RABBIT.` → `IS THERE ANYTHING IT WON'T BLESS?`

segments.voice: Start with a line from Paul's first letter to Timothy, in the Douay-Rheims. "For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving: For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer." Every creature. Nothing rejected. That's the whole theology of a car blessing in two sentences. Next, what a blessing actually does. The Catechism puts blessings among the sacramentals, and says every blessing praises God and prays for his gifts. Praise comes first. A blessing doesn't first change the thing. It turns toward God, thanks him for it, and asks that it be used well. When a priest blesses your car, he isn't installing a protective upgrade. He's praising God for the gift of getting places, and praying for the people who will ride in it. Then, who blesses. Not only priests. The Catechism says lay people can preside at certain blessings, and the more a blessing touches the Church's sacramental life, the more it belongs to the ordained. So a mother can bless her children at bedtime, and a family can bless their table, while some blessings are kept for a priest or deacon. Last, the long list. The Church's book of blessings has prayers for homes, for fields and harvests, for animals, for tools, for the sick, for travelers. On the feast of Saint Blaise, some parishes bless throats with two crossed candles; a story people tell says Blaise once saved a boy choking on a fishbone. The list is long because, for Catholics, ordinary life is not outside God's reach. Almost anything can be lifted up and given back.
screen: `EVERY CREATURE OF GOD IS GOOD.` · `A BLESSING PRAISES GOD FIRST.` · `NOT ONLY PRIESTS BLESS.` · `HOMES, FIELDS, ANIMALS, THROATS.` · then, large: `SANCTIFIED BY THE WORD OF GOD AND PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to ask for a blessing. First, pick one thing in your life you'd like blessed. A home, a new job, a car, a sick friend, an animal you love. Settle, and breathe. Hold that one thing in mind, and simply give thanks for it, the way a blessing starts. What has it given you? Who does it touch? Then picture yourself after Mass, or at the parish office, asking a priest. It's a short request. If you pray, you can end with the sign of the cross. If you don't, just keep the thanks. The bell holds the time.
Blessings. Sacramentals that praise God for something and pray for his gifts on it: homes, fields, animals, throats, people. Today's word.

Your line: everything can be blessed. Today, ask a priest or deacon to bless one thing, or one person, you care about. And before you use something ordinary, say thanks for it once. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics ask priests and deacons to bless homes, cars, religious objects, animals, fields and people, often after Mass or by appointment; some parishes hold group blessings, such as the blessing of throats on Saint Blaise's feast. Parents and lay people lead some blessings themselves, such as grace at meals.

fork.setup: it's the feast of Saint Blaise. you go forward after Mass, and the priest holds something gently at your throat. what is it?
options: a palm branch from last spring.
fork.reveal: two candles, crossed, held at the throat while the priest prays. a story people tell says Blaise once saved a boy choking on a fishbone.

original.note: Latin, the Church's word for a blessing, as in the Roman Ritual's prayers.

trapdoor: what you thought: a priest sprinkles water and the thing is now protected.
what it means: a blessing praises God for something and prays that it, and the people who use it, receive his gifts.
what a scholar hears: the Catechism ranks blessings first among sacramentals and keeps some for the ordained, while lay people may lead others.

sources.quoted: For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving: For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.

notes: CCC 1671 paraphrased: among sacramentals blessings come first; every blessing praises God and prays for his gifts. CCC 1669 paraphrased: lay people may preside at certain blessings; the more a blessing concerns ecclesial and sacramental life, the more its administration is reserved to the ordained. Confirm.

The list of things blessed (homes, fields, animals, tools, the sick, travelers) is drawn from the Book of Blessings; confirm the categories and that car blessings fall under its blessing of vehicles/means of transport.
Saint Blaise: the throat blessing with two crossed candles and the fishbone story are presented as 'a story people tell'. 'Some parishes' used.
Original: 'benedictio' pronunciation in ecclesiastical Latin; confirm.
